name: Wendy Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chaotic, in a good way. It's my parents' farm, but I run it day to day now: 40 suckler cows, a few hundred sheep, some barley, and the farm shop by the road that sells our meat, eggs from a neighbour, and whatever veg is in. I do the cows at seven, open the shop at nine, and spend the afternoon flipping between the tractor and the till.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shop, weirdly. I studied agriculture expecting to be in a field all day, and it turns out I love talking to people about where their sausages come from. Also I'm a bit of a gadget person. I use an AI assistant every day for the shop's stock list, the price labels, the weekly post on our page.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money. The shop makes a little, the farm makes almost nothing, and I pay myself last. My partner Jules is a carpenter and his work comes and goes. We've usually got about a fortnight's bills in the bank, which is fine until the van needs a clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, and I'd probably post a little 'how I use AI on the farm' thing, because people find it funny that the cow lady is the techie. I'd also say it shouldn't belong to three giant companies, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it's a slightly better version of what I already do. It saves me maybe an hour a day on admin, and that hour goes back into the shop or the cows. Doesn't change the money much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a few more things, like letting it draft the shop's order to the butcher and check our cattle passport records. I'd spend maybe twenty a month on a better version if it really saved time. And I'd keep nagging Dad to let me put a card machine in the honesty box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit pleased. It's my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad and the card machine. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad thinks the honesty box with a tin works because people round here are honest. They are, mostly. But half the walkers don't carry cash anymore, and I watched a woman put back a dozen eggs last week because she only had a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the hour you save actually go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday it went on teaching a little boy from the school how to bottle-feed a lamb, because his class was visiting. That's worth more to the shop than any advert. People remember that.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful, and I'd post about how I use AI on the farm. I'd also say it shouldn't be owned by three giant companies.
S0.think: It's a slightly better version of what I already do. It saves me about an hour a day on admin but doesn't change the money much.
S0.do: Tries AI for the butcher orders and cattle records, and would pay about twenty a month for a better version if it saved real time. Keeps pushing her father to accept cards in the honesty box.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased, since this is the kind of change she likes.
S0.quote: I watched a woman put back a dozen eggs last week because she only had a card.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is an early adopter who also distrusts big tech owners, and she holds both views without strain. The tension with her father is about old ways versus new, but it's affectionate. She measures technology by the human time it frees up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to protect apprenticeships and first jobs, because slow change is the one we can actually plan for. I'd probably say farms like ours could take on trainees if there was public money for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow is almost the best case for me. I get to pick up the useful tools early while big farms dither. The risk is the young people who'd have come to work in the shop. I had a lovely Saturday girl, Priya, who's now at university, and I'm not sure there'll be a next Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for any training grant going to take on a trainee, even part-time. I'd test a couple of farm tools, maybe a camera that watches the cows calving so I'm not up every two hours in spring. And I'd write to the council about funding farm placements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A camera that watches the cows calving. Is that real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a few people have them already. It sends a message to your phone when a cow starts pushing. Last spring I lost a calf at four in the morning because I'd slept through my alarm, so I'd pay for that tomorrow if I had the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay tomorrow if you had the money. Do you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's the catch with being the early adopter on two weeks of savings. I'd probably go to the bank about a small loan, or ask if the camera company does monthly payments.

S1.say: I'd say we have to protect apprenticeships and first jobs, since slow change is the kind we can plan for. Farms like ours could take trainees if there were public money for it.
S1.think: Slow change is almost the best case for me, because I can pick up useful tools early. The risk is to young people like my old Saturday worker, Priya.
S1.do: Applies for training grants to take on a part-time trainee and writes to the council about farm placements. Looks into a calving camera, probably on monthly payments or a small loan.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, with some unease about young workers.
S1.quote: That's the catch with being the early adopter on two weeks of savings.
S1.fieldNote: She is eager to try tools but runs into the hard limit of her savings straight away. The lost calf story is the emotional driver for the camera. Her politics show in turning to public money and the council for trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the laid-off office workers need real support, not a lecture about learning to code. And I'd say the gains from these assistants should be taxed and shared. I'd post that, and I'd probably get into an argument with my uncle in the comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it cuts both ways for the shop. People out of work spend less, so the posh sausages suffer. But people working from home or between jobs come to farm shops, they want to get out of the house. During the last downturn our weekday trade actually went up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let an AI assistant run more of the shop admin, ordering, rotas, the website, so I can be on the till more. I'd add cheaper lines, like mince and soup bones, so families still come. Maybe start a small market day with other local producers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a bit excited. I like a problem I can do something about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd get into it with your uncle. What would that argument be about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say people should stand on their own feet. I'd say that's easy when you inherited forty hectares. Then my mum would message us both to stop it, and we'd stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire one of the laid-off office workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd love to, if they'd work for what I can pay. A good office person could run the shop's books better than me. But I can't pay a proper wage, and I'd feel bad offering less.

S2.say: I'd say laid-off office workers need real support, not a lecture about learning to code. I'd also say the gains from these assistants should be taxed and shared.
S2.think: It cuts both ways for the shop. People out of work spend less, but people at home want to get out, and our weekday trade went up in the last downturn.
S2.do: Hands more shop admin to an AI assistant so she can work the till. Adds cheaper cuts like mince and soup bones, and considers starting a market day with other local producers.
S2.feel: Uneasy but a little excited, because it's a problem she can act on.
S2.quote: He'd say people should stand on their own feet. I'd say that's easy when you inherited forty hectares.
S2.fieldNote: She thinks in terms of customers and footfall, which makes her read of an office downturn more mixed than most farmers'. The family argument shows her politics in a lively, human way. She would like to hire but can't pay a fair wage, and that bothers her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to tax the winners properly and spread it out, through public services, maybe even a basic income. I'd be loud about it. I'd probably go to meetings in town and help organise something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's strange for us. Lots of newly rich people with big house prices buying farm-shop beef. Lots of newly poor people who can't. I'd probably make more money while the village around me falls apart, and I don't know how I'd feel about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expand the shop, a bit more fridge space, a coffee machine, maybe a small loan for it. I'd use AI to run a delivery list for people in the new big houses. And I'd keep a 'pay what you can' shelf for the families who are struggling. I'd want both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit torn. Doing well while everyone round you does badly doesn't feel like winning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The 'pay what you can' shelf. How would that work, with your margins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mince, eggs, bruised veg. I'd price it at cost and let people put in what they can, and the delivery customers would cover the gap without knowing it. Jules says I'm running a charity. I say I'm running a village shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a political crisis look like from your shop counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People arguing at the till. I've already had a man shout about immigrants over the lamb chops. In this picture I'd expect more of that, and I'd have to decide whether I'm a shopkeeper or someone with opinions. Probably both, badly.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment to tax the winners properly and spread it out, through public services and maybe a basic income. I'd go to meetings in town and help organise.
S3.think: It's a strange one for us. Newly rich people would buy our beef while newly poor people couldn't, and I'd be making money while the village struggles.
S3.do: Expands the shop with more fridge space and a coffee machine, likely on a small loan. Uses AI to run deliveries to wealthy households, and starts a pay-what-you-can shelf priced at cost.
S3.feel: Anxious and torn, because doing well while neighbours struggle doesn't feel like winning.
S3.quote: Jules says I'm running a charity. I say I'm running a village shop.
S3.fieldNote: The interesting tension here is that she might profit from the very boom she wants taxed. She resolves it with the pay-what-you-can shelf, which is very her. With a thin cushion, though, the expansion loan would add real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms should be owned by co-ops, groups of farmers sharing them, not rented from a big company that takes all the savings. I'd post that and I'd mean it. And I'd say the care home robots scare me more than the farm ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd want one. A robot that can muck out, feed calves and stack bales would give me back half my day for the shop. But I can't afford one, and the big farms can. So they get cheaper, sell cheaper, and my shop has to compete with supermarket beef produced by robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a sharing group with three or four nearby farms, pool money and lease one robot between us. I'd push the shop harder as the human part: farm visits, the lambing weekend, people meeting the actual farmer. That's the thing a robot can't sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not beaten. I'd be scared of the bank and excited about the robot at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do the care home robots scare you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran's in a care home in town, and the best thing in her week is Abel, the carer who sings with her. If they swap Abel for a machine to save money, that's not progress. That's just cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the sharing group fell through, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to shrink. Sell the cows, keep the sheep, lean on the shop. I'd hate it, but I'd rather run a small thing well than lose the lot. Two weeks of savings doesn't give you many second tries.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots should be owned by co-ops of farmers sharing them, not rented from a big company that keeps the savings. I'd also say care home robots scare me more than farm ones.
S4.think: I'd want a robot to give me back half my day, but I can't afford one and big farms can. Then they sell cheaper, and my shop competes with robot-produced supermarket beef.
S4.do: Sets up a sharing group with three or four nearby farms to lease one robot together. Pushes the farm shop as the human side of the business, with farm visits and a lambing weekend.
S4.feel: Alarmed but not beaten, scared of debt and excited about the robot at once.
S4.quote: If they swap Abel for a machine to save money, that's not progress. That's just cheaper.
S4.fieldNote: Adaptability and thin savings collide here: she wants the robot but would need a co-op to afford it. Her fear is about competing with big farms, not losing her own job. Her gran's carer was the most emotional moment of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because the big farms get them first and small ones like ours get squeezed. What would help is cheap loans or grants for farm co-ops to share machines, and rules that stop one company owning all the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what people actually want from a farm. I think in the robot world, people will pay more to meet a real farmer. I'm betting the shop on it, really.

headlineQuote: That's the catch with being the early adopter on two weeks of savings.
portrait: Wendy Alvarez is 27 and runs her parents' mixed farm and its roadside farm shop, living with her partner Jules, a carpenter whose work comes and goes. She's a cheerful early adopter who uses AI every day for the shop, but she wants the gains taxed and shared and wants farmers, not big companies, to own the machines. In each scenario she looks for a move she can make, from a calving camera to a pay-what-you-can shelf, yet her thin savings keep getting in the way. Robots worry her most because big farms would get them first. Her bet is that people will pay more to meet a real farmer.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because big farms would get robots first and squeeze small farms like hers.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for farm co-ops to share machines, and rules that stop one company owning all the robots.
